READING

**The numbers at stake**

Start with the plain rent arithmetic. ARDENSHAW costs £214,000 a year for ten years = £2,140,000 in new-lease rent. KESTERWICK costs £118,000 a year for ten years = £1,180,000. Gross saving: £960,000.

Against that, KESTERWICK spends:
- Works: £480,000
- Dead mileage (see below): ~£260,000 over ten years
- Deposit: £40,000 if the decision slips past 5 December; £0 if decided before then

Net advantage to KESTERWICK before any Nethercote exposure: roughly £220,000 (no deposit) to £180,000 (with deposit). That is real money but not a knockout. The question is whether the risks eat it.

**Dead mileage**

Culverstone adds 3 miles each way to get 22 vehicles to/from the Verrancombe Bridge stand. Round trip extra = 6 miles per vehicle per day.

22 vehicles × 313 days × 6 miles × £0.63 = **£26,030 per year**, £260,300 over ten years.

That is already in the figure above. It does not eliminate the KESTERWICK advantage.

**Planning timeline — the critical path**

The application was validated 2026-08-14. Working from that date:

| Scenario | Consent | +22 weeks construction | Ready |
|---|---|---|---|
| Published target (13 wk) | 2026-11-13 | +22 wk | 2027-04-08 |
| Median (34 wk) | 2027-04-09 | +22 wk | 2027-09-10 |
| Worst recorded (61 wk) | 2027-10-15 | +22 wk | 2028-03-05 |

Hallowbrand lease ends **2027-11-30**.

- Best case: Culverstone ready April 2027. No gap; they could even rationalise out of Hallowbrand early.
- Median case: Culverstone ready September 2027. Eleven weeks before Hallowbrand ends. Move across smoothly.
- Worst case: Culverstone ready March 2028. Gap of roughly three months after the Hallowbrand lease expires.

By definition more than half of determinations beat the median, so better than 50% probability of a smooth transition. The tail risk is real but bounded.

**Nethercote exposure in the worst case**

Three to four months at £18,500/month = roughly £55,000–£74,000. No workshop during that period is operationally uncomfortable for a 31-vehicle fleet (maintenance must be contracted out), but it is not existential: Nethercote is available month to month and the Culverstone option remains valid to 2028-06-30. Add £74,000 worst-case Nethercote to KESTERWICK costs and the ten-year advantage is still roughly £106,000–£146,000.

**The deposit decision and timing**

Today is 25 August 2026. The free hold on Culverstone runs to 5 December 2026. Hallowbrand answer is due 19 December 2026. If the board decides KESTERWICK in the next few weeks it avoids the £40,000 deposit entirely. That is available to them and should not be left on the table.

**Cash adequacy**

Cash: £640,000. Works: £480,000. Remaining after works: £160,000 in cash plus £200,000 undrawn = £360,000 available buffer. Works do not need to be paid on day one — they follow consent, which is months away — so in practice the cash position is more comfortable than the static comparison suggests. The business continues generating cash from school contracts and private hire in the interim. KESTERWICK does not threaten solvency.

**The bid — the factor that tips the scales**

The 44/44A bid is due 2027-09-14. Depot cost enters as a fixed line.

Under ARDENSHAW that line is £214,000 — signed, certain, but a heavy number.

Under KESTERWICK median scenario, Culverstone is occupied by September 2027 and the line is £118,000. That is a £96,000/year reduction in the cost base priced into the bid. On a contract for 22 vehicles that represents the majority of the business, a cost advantage of that magnitude is not a marginal rounding error — it is the kind of number that decides competitive tenders. A contract loss in 2028 would be a far larger financial event than anything in the KESTERWICK risk column.

Under the worst-case planning scenario, consent comes in October 2027 — after the bid date. In that scenario the management team would have to bid on the basis of Culverstone at £118,000 (they hold the option to June 2028; the site is practically certain to be delivered). That introduces some residual uncertainty, but the bid is not made blind: they know the site, the costs, and the timeline.

**Planning refusal**

The problem provides no probability for refusal. Hardstanding, a fuel island and a two-bay workshop on what is presumably an industrial or commercial site is not an inherently difficult consent class. Were refusal material there would presumably be something to flag. I treat the planning risk as primarily timing risk rather than outcome risk, while noting that the board should ensure a fallback position is understood.

**ARDENSHAW's case, stated fairly**

It is not nothing. Certainty has genuine value. No capital tied up in leasehold improvements. No workshop dark period. Bid priced to the penny. The landlord's £214,000 is expensive but it is also a known quantity for planning, budgeting and contract purposes through to 2037. If the business's priority is absolute operational continuity and minimum capital exposure, ARDENSHAW is defensible.

But it locks the company into paying £96,000 more per year than the alternative — £960,000 more over the decade — for a leasehold interest in someone else's site, at the end of which nothing has been built and the position is the same or worse.

**Synthesis**

KESTERWICK is financially better in every scenario that does not involve planning refusal, and even the worst recorded determination (61 weeks) leaves the Culverstone option intact and produces a gap manageable with Nethercote. The decisive asymmetry is the bid: arriving at the September 2027 tender with a £118,000 depot line rather than a £214,000 one could be the difference between retaining or losing the network that runs 22 of 31 vehicles. The cost of being wrong about planning timing is bounded and costed; the cost of losing the 44/44A contract is not.

The decision should be taken before 5 December to avoid the deposit.

---

READING
  Rent differential over ten years: £960,000. Works: £480,000. Dead mileage: £260,000. Net advantage to KESTERWICK before any Nethercote exposure: ~£220,000. Worst-case Nethercote (3–4 months): ~£74,000. Residual advantage: ~£146,000. Cash is adequate — £640,000 in hand, works paid against a timeline months away, £200,000 facility undrawn. Planning timing risk is real (13–61 weeks, median 34) but in the median and better cases Culverstone is ready before Hallowbrand ends; the worst case produces a temporary Nethercote stay that is inconvenient but costed and bounded. Culverstone is held to June 2028, well past any plausible build-out. The decisive factor is the 44/44A bid due 2027-09-14: depot cost enters as a fixed line, and arriving with £118,000 rather than £214,000 — a £96,000/year gap — on a contract running 22 of 31 vehicles is a competitive advantage that directly affects whether the business retains its core revenue base. Deciding KESTERWICK before 5 December 2026 also saves the £40,000 deposit. ARDENSHAW offers real certainty but at a price that over ten years exceeds the entire Culverstone construction cost almost twice, and it forfeits the bid advantage permanently.

CALL
  KESTERWICK

GROUNDS
  The £96,000-per-year saving in depot cost, flowing directly into the September 2027 contract bid as a fixed line, provides a competitive advantage that could determine whether Trentmoor retains the 44/44A network, and the ten-year financial benefit remains materially positive even when the full cost of works, dead mileage and a worst-case Nethercote interlude are set against it.
